Astral announced ty's beta on 2025-12-16; it is still 0.0.x (0.0.84, 2026-09-24) and its README still says beta

corrections.verdict: confirmed (the --package flag is now the default behaviour)

Code that needs C++20 must ask for it

PyO3 0.29.3 (2026-09-30); `maturin new` on maturin 1.15.0 writes `pyo3 = "0.29.0"`

jobs.label: Install the language
jobs.q: How do I get the compiler or interpreter, in the version I want, without breaking the system one?

jobs.label: Project and dependencies
jobs.q: How do I start a project and add a library to it?

jobs.label: Lockfile
jobs.q: Which file pins the exact versions, so my laptop and CI build the same thing?

jobs.label: Formatter
jobs.q: What rewrites my code into the one house style?

jobs.label: Linter
jobs.q: What warns about code that is legal but probably wrong?

jobs.label: Type checker
jobs.q: What checks types before the program runs?

jobs.label: Test runner
jobs.q: How do I write and run tests?

jobs.label: Build system
jobs.q: What turns source files into something that runs or installs?

jobs.label: Debugger and profiler
jobs.q: How do I stop the program and look inside, and find where the time goes?

jobs.label: Sanitizers and memory checkers
jobs.q: What catches memory bugs and undefined behaviour while the program runs?

jobs.label: Documentation
jobs.q: How do comments in the code become a documentation site?

jobs.label: Publishing a package
jobs.q: How do I put my library where others can install it?

jobs.label: Calling the other languages
jobs.q: How does this language call, or get called by, the other three?

jobs.label: Notebooks and REPL
jobs.q: Where do I try one line interactively?

py.sum: Let uv download standalone CPython builds per project; leave the system Python alone.
py.warn: Two interpreters can sit on one machine (system, Homebrew, uv); `which python` tells you which one a bare `python` runs.

tools.what: uv downloads and manages CPython builds (from python-build-standalone) per user, and pins one per project with .python-version.
The reference interpreter itself; 3.14 is the current bugfix line and 3.15.0 is due 2026-10-09.
The older shell-based version manager that compiles Python from source.

cpp.sum: No version manager: you install a compiler from the OS or vendor and pick the language standard with a flag.
cpp.py: There is no uv python for C++. The closest thing to choosing a Python version is the -std=c++20 flag (or CMAKE_CXX_STANDARD), which picks the language standard the compiler follows.
cpp.warn: The default standard differs by compiler and version. Measured on this Mac: Apple clang 14.0.0 defaults to C++98 (__cplusplus 199711L), Apple clang 17.0.0 to C++14; upstream Clang 16+ and GCC 11+ default to C++17, GCC 16 to C++20. Always pass the standard.

tools.what: The LLVM project's C and C++ compiler; Apple's Xcode clang is a separate fork with its own version numbers.
tools.cmd: brew install llvm   (or xcode-select --install for Apple clang)

tools.what: The GNU compiler collection, the default C++ compiler on most Linux distributions; GCC 16 made C++20 its default mode.
Microsoft's compiler, installed with Visual Studio or the standalone Build Tools.
tools.cmd: Visual Studio Installer, workload 'Desktop development with C++'

rs.sum: rustup installs and switches toolchains (stable, beta, nightly, or a pinned version) per user or per folder.
rs.py: rustup is to rustc what uv python is to CPython; a rust-toolchain.toml file in a repo plays the part of .python-version.
rs.warn: Some tools (Miri, -Z flags, the sanitizers) need the nightly toolchain: rustup toolchain install nightly, then cargo +nightly ...

tools.what: The official toolchain installer: puts rustc, cargo and the standard library in your home folder and updates them.
The compiler and its build tool, released together every six weeks.

ts.sum: Install a JavaScript runtime (Node, Bun or Deno); TypeScript itself is a per-project npm package, not something you install globally.
ts.py: The runtime is the interpreter (like CPython); nvm is the pyenv of Node. TypeScript is a dev dependency, like ruff: each project pins its own compiler in package.json.
ts.warn: Production should run an LTS line (24 now; 26 becomes LTS on 2026-10-28). Odd-numbered lines were never LTS; from Node 27 every major will be.

tools.what: The default JavaScript runtime, built on Chrome's V8 engine; even-numbered lines get long-term support (LTS).
A shell script that installs and switches Node versions per shell.
Faster version managers written in Rust; mise also manages Python, Rust and other tools from one file.
An all-in-one runtime, package manager, bundler and test runner on JavaScriptCore; owned by Anthropic since December 2025, rewritten in Rust in 1.4.
A runtime from Node's original author with permissions off by default and TypeScript built in.

py.sum: uv creates the project, adds dependencies to pyproject.toml, and keeps the environment in sync.
py.warn: Astral, uv's maker, agreed to join OpenAI (announced 2026-03-19); uv stays MIT and Apache licensed.

tools.what: One Rust binary that replaces pip, venv, pip-tools, pipx and pyenv, with a lockfile.
tools.cmd: uv init myproj && uv add httpx

tools.what: The installer that ships with Python; installs into whatever environment is active and does not lock.
The first popular all-in-one project tool, still common in existing repositories.
The package manager for the conda-forge ecosystem, which also ships non-Python binaries such as CUDA toolkits and compilers.
A Rust project manager for conda-forge packages with a lockfile, the uv of the conda world.

cpp.sum: No standard tool. A build system (CMake) plus, optionally, a package manager (vcpkg or Conan) that feeds it libraries.
cpp.py: Imagine Python with no pip and no PyPI, where every project chooses its own way to fetch C libraries: that is C++. vcpkg.json is the closest thing to the dependencies list in pyproject.toml.
cpp.warn: A compiled library must match your compiler, standard library, flags and architecture (its ABI). That, not laziness, is why C++ never got one registry.

tools.what: Microsoft's source-based package manager: a vcpkg.json manifest in your repo and a CMake toolchain file that makes find_package work.
tools.cmd: vcpkg new --application && vcpkg add port fmt

tools.what: A binary package manager (written in Python) whose profiles describe compiler, standard library and architecture, so it can ship prebuilt libraries that match your ABI.
A CMake module that downloads a dependency by git URL and tag and builds it with your project; no extra tool, no lockfile.
apt or Homebrew install headers and libraries machine-wide; simple, not reproducible.

rs.sum: cargo does everything: new project, add a dependency, build, test, publish.
rs.py: cargo is uv, pytest, the build backend and twine in one tool. Cargo.toml is pyproject.toml; cargo add is uv add.
rs.warn: For 0.x versions cargo treats the minor number as breaking: ^0.14 accepts 0.14.9 but not 0.15.0.

tools.what: Rust's build tool and package manager, shipped with every toolchain.
tools.cmd: cargo new myproj && cargo add serde

ts.sum: A package manager writes package.json and installs into node_modules/; npm ships with Node, pnpm and Bun are faster alternatives.
ts.py: package.json is pyproject.toml, node_modules/ is .venv (but per project, always), npm install is uv sync, npx is uvx.
ts.warn: npm install --save-dev puts a tool in devDependencies (like a uv dev group). The bundled npm follows Node: Node 22.22.2 shipped npm 10.9.7 here while the registry's latest npm is 12.2.0.

tools.what: The package manager bundled with Node.
A faster npm with a content-addressed store and stricter node_modules (a package sees only what it declares).
Bun's npm-compatible installer, usually the fastest.

py.sum: uv.lock pins every package with its hash; PEP 751 now defines a standard pylock.toml too.
py.warn: Applications commit the lockfile; libraries declare ranges and test their lower bounds.

tools.what: uv's cross-platform lockfile, written by uv add, uv lock and uv sync.
The standard lockfile format (PEP 751, status Final); uv can export to it.
A list of pins, often produced by pip freeze; a snapshot of what is installed, not a resolved lock.

cpp.sum: Only if you use a package manager: vcpkg pins a baseline commit of its registry, Conan writes conan.lock.
cpp.py: With system packages or FetchContent there is no lockfile at all; the git tag in FetchContent is the only pin.
cpp.warn: Pinning sources is half the job: the compiler version and flags also change the binary, so CI images pin the compiler too.

tools.what: A registry commit in vcpkg.json that fixes the version of every port, plus overrides for exact pins.
Conan's lockfile of exact package revisions.

rs.sum: Cargo.lock, written automatically on the first build.
rs.py: Cargo.lock is uv.lock. cargo build updates it when Cargo.toml changes, as uv run does for uv.lock.
rs.warn: cargo new tracks Cargo.lock in git by default; the Cargo FAQ says whether a library commits it depends on its needs, and a library's lockfile never affects the people who depend on it.

tools.what: The exact resolved version and checksum of every crate in the build.
tools.cmd: cargo update   (refresh within the allowed ranges)

ts.sum: Each package manager writes its own: package-lock.json, pnpm-lock.yaml or bun.lock.
ts.py: npm ci is uv sync --locked: install exactly what the lockfile says, or fail.
ts.warn: The three lockfiles are not interchangeable; a repo should have exactly one.

tools.what: npm's lockfile: exact version, tarball URL and integrity hash of every package in node_modules.
tools.cmd: npm ci   (install exactly the lockfile, for CI)

tools.what: pnpm's lockfile.
Bun's text lockfile (bun init wrote one in the walkthrough).

py.warn: A package's import name can differ from its PyPI name (pip install scikit-learn, import sklearn).

tools.what: The public registry of Python packages (wheels and source distributions).

cpp.sum: No central registry. Curated collections instead: the vcpkg ports in microsoft/vcpkg and ConanCenter.
cpp.py: Each collection is curated by pull request, so a library exists there only if someone wrote a recipe for it.

tools.what: Port recipes in the microsoft/vcpkg GitHub repository, tagged in dated releases.
Conan's central collection of recipes and prebuilt binaries.

rs.sum: crates.io; every published crate also gets documentation on docs.rs.
rs.py: crates.io is PyPI; docs.rs builds the API docs of every version automatically, which PyPI does not do.

tools.what: The public registry of Rust crates.

ts.sum: The npm registry; JSR is a newer TypeScript-first registry from the Deno team.
ts.py: The npm registry is PyPI. Packages ship JavaScript plus .d.ts type files; types for untyped packages come from DefinitelyTyped as @types/<name> (like types-requests for mypy).
ts.warn: Install scripts (postinstall) run arbitrary code at install time, as setup.py once did.

tools.what: The registry behind npm, pnpm, Yarn and Bun, the largest package registry there is.
A registry that accepts TypeScript source, generates docs and serves packages to npm, Deno and Bun.

py.sum: ruff format, a drop-in, much faster Black.

tools.what: Ruff's formatter, designed to match Black's output.
The formatter that made one style normal in Python.

cpp.sum: clang-format, configured by a .clang-format file in the repo.
cpp.py: Unlike ruff format there is no single house style: the project's .clang-format decides, so check one in.
cpp.warn: The PyPI wheel (clang-format 23.1.2 here) is a convenient way to get the same version on every machine.

tools.what: LLVM's formatter for C, C++ and CUDA, with named base styles (LLVM, Google, Chromium, Mozilla, WebKit).

rs.py: cargo fmt is ruff format; the style is fixed by the Rust style guide and editions.

tools.what: The official formatter, a rustup component.

ts.sum: Prettier is the long-time standard; Biome is a much faster Rust formatter and linter in one.
ts.py: Biome is the ruff of JavaScript: one fast Rust binary for formatting and linting.

tools.what: The formatter for JavaScript, TypeScript, JSON, CSS and Markdown.
A Rust tool that formats (Prettier-compatible) and lints in one binary.

py.sum: ruff check: hundreds of rules from flake8, isort, pyupgrade and others, in one Rust binary.

tools.what: Ruff's linter; --fix applies the safe automatic fixes.

cpp.sum: The compiler's own warnings first (-Wall -Wextra), then clang-tidy for deeper checks.
cpp.py: clang-tidy plays ruff check's part, but needs the exact compiler flags of each file, which is why the walkthrough exports compile_commands.json.

tools.what: -Wall -Wextra (and -Werror in CI) turn on the compiler's built-in checks; the cheapest linter there is.
LLVM's linter with checks grouped by family (bugprone-, modernize-, performance-, cppcoreguidelines-); reads compile_commands.json. Its PyPI wheel (22.1.8) trails LLVM 23.

rs.sum: clippy: about the language's idioms as much as its bugs.
rs.py: cargo clippy is ruff check. cargo clippy -- -W clippy::pedantic turns on the opinionated group, a fast way to learn idiomatic Rust.

tools.what: The official linter, a rustup component, with lints in groups such as correctness, style, complexity, perf and pedantic.

ts.sum: ESLint with typescript-eslint is the standard; Biome and Oxlint are faster Rust linters.
ts.warn: typescript-eslint uses the TypeScript compiler API, which TypeScript 7.0 does not have yet; Microsoft's 7.0 post says such tools keep running on TypeScript 6 side by side until the 7.1 API.

tools.what: The pluggable JavaScript linter; flat config (eslint.config.js) is the only format in ESLint 10.
The parser and rules that let ESLint read TypeScript and use type information.
Biome's built-in linter.
A Rust linter from the Oxc project that runs ESLint-style rules.

py.sum: Optional, separate checkers read your annotations; Python itself ignores them at run time.
py.seen_intro: One bug, four tools: count_tokens(42) where a str is expected. Python only fails when the line runs; all three checkers reject it before running, each in its own words.
py.warn: A clean check is per checker: the three differ on inference and strictness, so a project picks one and runs it in CI.

tools.what: The original Python type checker, now at major version 2 and releasing regularly.
Microsoft's checker (the engine behind Pylance), strict and fast, written in TypeScript.
Astral's checker and language server in Rust; in beta since 2025-12-16.

cpp.sum: The compiler is the type checker; there is no separate step and no way to skip it.
cpp.py: Like running mypy on every save with no way to ignore it, except that the errors come from template instantiation and can be long.

tools.what: Every build checks every type; templates are checked when instantiated, concepts (C++20) let you state requirements up front.

rs.sum: The compiler, including the borrow checker; cargo check runs it without producing a binary.
rs.py: cargo check is mypy that cannot be skipped and also checks lifetimes and data races.

tools.what: Type-checks and borrow-checks the crate without code generation, much faster than a build.
The language server that shows the same errors in your editor as you type; weekly releases.

ts.sum: tsc checks; since TypeScript 7.0 (2026-07-08) tsc is the native Go port, the project once called tsgo.
ts.seen_intro: Node runs TypeScript by deleting the types, so a wrong argument reaches run time; tsc stops it first (walkthrough files).
ts.py: tsc --noEmit is mypy for TypeScript, with one difference that matters: types are erased, so nothing checks them at run time, exactly as in Python.
ts.warn: Running a .ts file (node, bun, deno, tsx) does not type-check it. Keep npx tsc --noEmit in CI.

tools.what: The compiler and checker, rewritten in Go: the typescript package on npm and its tsc binary.
The last JavaScript-based compiler, kept for tools that need the compiler API; installs as @typescript/typescript6 with a tsc6 binary.
The preview package of the Go port; superseded by typescript 7, with nightlies moving to typescript@next.
Finds test_*.py files and test_ functions; fixtures and parametrize do the rest.
The standard library's xUnit-style framework; pytest runs these tests too.

cpp.sum: Pick a framework (GoogleTest or Catch2) and let CTest run the executables.
cpp.py: Tests are separate executables; a test is a compiled program that returns non-zero on failure.

tools.what: CMake's test driver: runs every executable registered with add_test.
Google's xUnit framework (TEST and EXPECT_EQ macros) plus gMock for mocks.
tools.cmd: FetchContent or vcpkg add port gtest

tools.what: A framework with natural REQUIRE(a == b) assertions and sections.

rs.sum: Built in: #[test] functions next to the code, cargo test runs them in parallel; doc examples are tests too.
rs.py: cargo test is pytest plus doctest, built in; assert_eq! is assert a == b with both values printed on failure.

tools.what: Builds and runs unit tests, integration tests in tests/, and the code examples in doc comments.
A faster runner that runs each test in its own process, with better output.

ts.sum: Vitest is the common choice; Node and Bun also have built-in runners.
ts.py: test() and expect(x).toBe(y) are pytest functions and assert x == y.

tools.what: A fast, Jest-compatible runner that understands TypeScript and ES modules without setup.
Node's built-in test runner, no dependency needed.
The long-time standard, still in many codebases.
Bun's built-in Jest-compatible runner.

py.sum: Pure Python needs no build to run; a build backend makes the wheel you publish, and compiled extensions use maturin or scikit-build-core.

tools.what: Builds a source distribution and a wheel using the backend named in pyproject.toml.
Build backends for pure-Python packages; uv init picks uv_build.
A backend that drives CMake to build C++ extensions into wheels.

cpp.sum: Two layers: a generator (CMake) describes the project, a fast executor (Ninja) runs the compiler; then the compiler and linker.
cpp.py: No Python equivalent: in Python the interpreter reads source directly. CMakeLists.txt is closest to pyproject.toml plus the build backend.
cpp.warn: Debug and Release are different builds (CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE); benchmark only Release.

tools.what: The de facto build description language; generates Ninja, Make or Visual Studio builds.
A small, fast build executor that runs only what changed.
A newer build description language in Python syntax, used by NumPy and SciPy (meson-python).

rs.sum: cargo build; rustc compiles each crate through LLVM.
rs.py: No separate build system to learn: Cargo.toml describes it all. build.rs scripts handle the odd C dependency.
rs.warn: The default debug profile is unoptimised; never time a debug build (the Benchmark tab uses --release).

tools.what: Builds the crate and its dependencies; --release turns on optimisation.

ts.sum: Often none: Node, Bun and Deno run .ts directly. tsc emits JavaScript when you need it; bundlers package code for browsers or for shipping.
ts.warn: Node's built-in stripping runs only erasable syntax: enums, namespaces with runtime code, parameter properties and import aliases throw (Node docs, Modules: TypeScript); tsx or a build handles them.

tools.what: Emits .js and .d.ts files from .ts (or only checks, with noEmit).
A Go bundler and transpiler, the engine under many tools.
The dev server and bundler for web front ends.
Runs a .ts file with full TypeScript syntax support (enums, decorators) without a build step.

py.sum: pdb or the editor's debugger to step; py-spy or the new Tachyon profiler to sample a running program.

tools.what: The standard library debugger; breakpoint() in the code stops there.
The debug adapter behind VS Code's Python debugger.
A sampling profiler in Rust that attaches to a running process without changing it.
A CPU, memory and GPU profiler that separates time in Python from time in native code.
Python 3.15's built-in sampling profiler (PEP 799); attach by PID or run a script.

cpp.sum: gdb on Linux, lldb on macOS; perf (Linux) or Instruments (macOS) for profiles.
cpp.py: Build with -g (debug info) so the debugger can map machine code back to your lines; CMake's Debug build does that.
cpp.warn: Optimised builds reorder and delete code, so stepping a Release build jumps around; use RelWithDebInfo to profile with symbols.

tools.what: LLVM's debugger, the default on macOS.
The GNU debugger, the default on Linux.
The Linux kernel's sampling profiler; versioned with the kernel.
Apple's profiler, part of Xcode.

rs.sum: The same native debuggers through rustup's wrappers; cargo flamegraph or samply for profiles.

tools.what: lldb and gdb with pretty-printers for Rust types, installed with the toolchain.
Profiles a run and writes a flame graph SVG (uses perf or dtrace).
A sampling profiler that opens the result in the Firefox Profiler.

ts.sum: node --inspect connects Chrome DevTools or VS Code; the same DevTools record CPU and heap profiles.
ts.py: --inspect-brk is breakpoint() on the first line; DevTools' Performance panel is py-spy with a GUI.

tools.what: Starts Node with the V8 inspector, so Chrome DevTools or VS Code can set breakpoints.
Writes a .cpuprofile you open in DevTools.

py.sum: Pure Python cannot corrupt memory, so there is little to sanitize; dev mode, faulthandler and memory profilers cover the rest.
py.warn: Memory bugs in Python programs live in C or C++ extensions; finding them takes the C++ tools in the next column (an ASan build of the extension).

tools.what: Development mode: extra runtime checks, ResourceWarnings shown, faulthandler on.
The standard library module that records where memory was allocated.
Bloomberg's memory profiler that also sees allocations inside C extensions.

cpp.sum: Compile with -fsanitize=address, undefined or thread and run the tests; the program then reports the bug at the line that caused it.
cpp.seen_intro: Signed integer overflow is undefined behaviour in C++. Without a sanitizer the program prints a wrapped number and exits 0; with UBSan it names the line (walk/overflow.cpp, Apple clang 14.0.0).
cpp.warn: Measured limit of this machine: ASan could not run here (Apple clang 14.0.0 reported 'Interceptors are not working', Apple clang 17.0.0's ASan build hung at start on macOS 27), so no ASan output is shown; UBSan worked. Sanitizers are most reliable on Linux CI.
cpp.py: A sanitizer turns 'it printed something odd' into an error with a line number, which is what Python gives you by default.

tools.what: Detects use-after-free, buffer overflow and leaks at about 2x slowdown, per the Clang documentation.
Reports undefined behaviour such as signed overflow and misaligned access at run time.
Detects data races between threads.
Runs an unmodified binary on a simulated CPU to find memory errors; much slower, Linux mostly.

rs.sum: Safe Rust rules out these bugs at compile time; for unsafe code, Miri interprets the program and reports undefined behaviour.
rs.seen_intro: The C++ dangling-pointer bug in Rust (walk/walk_miri.sh). With a reference, the compiler refuses it; with a raw pointer in unsafe, it compiles and prints a stale value; Miri catches it.
rs.py: Most Rust code needs no sanitizer, the way most Python code does not: the compiler already said no.

tools.what: Rejects code that could use freed memory or race, before it runs.
An interpreter for Rust's mid-level IR that detects undefined behaviour in unsafe code; nightly only.
tools.cmd: rustup +nightly component add miri && cargo +nightly miri test

tools.what: The same ASan and TSan as C++, through a nightly-only compiler flag.

ts.sum: No sanitizers: the runtime is memory-safe and garbage collected. Leaks (objects kept alive by mistake) are found with heap snapshots.
ts.py: Same as Python: no use-after-free is possible, so the memory question is only 'what is still referenced?'

tools.what: DevTools' Memory panel, through node --inspect, compares snapshots to find what keeps objects alive.
Writes a heap snapshot automatically when the process is about to run out of memory.

py.sum: Docstrings, rendered by Sphinx or MkDocs (with mkdocstrings), or pdoc for a quick API site.

tools.what: The documentation generator behind docs.python.org and most scientific libraries.
Markdown-based sites; Material for MkDocs is the common theme.
Generates API docs from docstrings and type hints with no configuration.

cpp.sum: Doxygen comments (/// or /** */) rendered by Doxygen.

tools.what: Extracts comments from headers into HTML or XML (Sphinx can read the XML through Breathe).

rs.sum: /// comments in Markdown, built by cargo doc; docs.rs hosts every published version.
rs.py: cargo doc --open is a local docs.rs: you get your dependencies' docs offline, at the exact versions you use.

tools.what: Builds HTML docs for your crate and every dependency; code blocks in doc comments run as tests.
Builds books from Markdown; The Rust Book is made with it.

ts.sum: TSDoc or JSDoc comments rendered by TypeDoc; JSR builds docs automatically.
ts.py: The .d.ts files a package ships are its machine-readable API, like a py.typed package's stubs; editors show them as docs on hover.

tools.what: Generates an API site from TypeScript types and doc comments.
Every package published to JSR gets generated docs and a documentation score.

py.sum: uv build then uv publish to PyPI, ideally with trusted publishing from CI (no API token stored).

tools.what: Uploads the built sdist and wheels to PyPI or another index.
The older standard upload tool.
Builds wheels for every OS and Python version in CI, for packages with compiled code.

cpp.sum: No central upload. You tag a source release; to be installable, someone adds a recipe by pull request to vcpkg's ports or ConanCenter.
cpp.py: Imagine publishing a Python library by sending a pull request to a curated list. Header-only libraries exist largely to avoid this step.

tools.what: A portfile and vcpkg.json under ports/<name> in the microsoft/vcpkg repository, merged by pull request.
A conanfile.py; conan create builds and tests the package locally, conan upload pushes it to a remote you control.

rs.sum: cargo publish, after cargo login with a crates.io token.
rs.py: One command where Python needs uv build plus uv publish. As on PyPI, a version number can never be reused.

tools.what: Packages the crate, verifies it builds, and uploads it to crates.io; a published version cannot be overwritten, only yanked (hidden from new resolutions).

ts.sum: npm publish to the npm registry, with provenance from CI; npx jsr publish for JSR.
ts.warn: A TypeScript library must ship JavaScript plus .d.ts files (or publish to JSR), and the exports field in package.json decides what importers can reach.

tools.what: Uploads the package; --provenance links it to the CI build that made it.
Publishes TypeScript source to JSR, which compiles it for npm consumers.

py.sum: Python is the host: Rust comes in through PyO3 and maturin, C++ through nanobind or pybind11, C through ctypes or cffi; JavaScript only via a subprocess or a WebAssembly runtime.
py.seen_intro: Rust called from Python, run for real: maturin made the project, built a CPython 3.14 wheel of the Rust count_tokens and installed it; Python then imported it like any module (walk/walk_pyo3.sh).

tools.what: PyO3 writes the Python module in Rust; maturin builds and installs it as a wheel.
C++17 bindings from the author of pybind11: smaller binaries and faster calls.
The incumbent C++ binding library, used by PyTorch's extension API.
Call a C shared library without compiling a module: ctypes ships with Python, cffi parses C declarations.

cpp.sum: C++ talks to everything through a C interface (extern "C"), or is wrapped by each host's binding tool.
cpp.py: PyTorch is the example: C++ (and CUDA) underneath, bound to Python with pybind11.

tools.what: Expose C++ classes and functions to Python.
Safe C++ and Rust interop: one bridge module declares both sides, checked at compile time.
C++ wrappers for Node's stable N-API, to write Node native addons.
Compiles C++ to WebAssembly so it runs in browsers and JavaScript runtimes.

rs.sum: Rust has a binding crate for each host: PyO3 for Python, napi-rs for Node, cxx and bindgen for C++, wasm-bindgen for the web.
rs.seen_intro: The same PyO3 run from the Rust side: the #[pyfunction] is the plain Rust count_tokens from the walkthrough with one attribute added.

tools.what: Rust to Python: the route pydantic-core, tokenizers and polars use (uv and ruff also ship their Rust binaries as wheels built by maturin).
Rust to Node native addons with generated TypeScript types.
Generates Rust declarations from C (and some C++) headers.
Compile Rust to WebAssembly with JavaScript glue.

ts.sum: JavaScript calls native code through Node-API addons (written in C++ or Rust), WebAssembly, or the runtime's FFI (bun:ffi, Deno.dlopen).
ts.py: A Node-API addon is a compiled extension module, exactly like a .so a Python wheel ships.

tools.what: Prebuilt native modules loaded by require or import; usually built with napi-rs (Rust) or node-addon-api (C++).
Load a .wasm module compiled from Rust or C++; works in Node, Bun, Deno and browsers.
Call a C shared library directly from Bun or Deno without writing an addon.

py.sum: The built-in REPL (colourful since 3.13), IPython, and notebooks: Jupyter or marimo.

tools.what: Type python; 3.13 brought colour, multi-line editing and paste mode.
An enhanced REPL with magics such as %timeit.
Notebooks in the browser.
Reactive notebooks stored as plain .py files.

cpp.sum: No everyday REPL. Compiler Explorer (godbolt.org) is the usual scratchpad; clang-repl and xeus-cpp exist.
cpp.py: The edit, compile, run loop replaces the REPL; keep a scratch CMake project or use godbolt.

tools.what: A website that compiles a snippet with many compilers and shows the assembly next to the source.
LLVM's interactive C++ interpreter, built on Clang's incremental compilation.

rs.sum: No built-in REPL. The Rust Playground runs snippets online; evcxr gives a REPL and a Jupyter kernel.

tools.what: Run and share snippets on play.rust-lang.org, with Clippy, Miri and the assembly view.
A Rust REPL and Jupyter kernel that compiles each line behind the scenes.

ts.sum: node starts a JavaScript REPL; Deno's REPL and Jupyter kernel accept TypeScript.
ts.py: The browser's DevTools console is also a JavaScript REPL, always one keypress away.

tools.what: Type node; it evaluates JavaScript (not TypeScript) line by line.
A TypeScript-aware REPL and a Jupyter kernel from the Deno runtime.

items.n: f-string grammar (PEP 701), type statement and generic syntax (PEP 695), per-interpreter GIL in the C API (PEP 684). Security fixes only as of 2026-10-05; end of life 2028-10.
New interactive REPL, experimental free-threaded build (PEP 703) and experimental JIT (PEP 744). Security fixes only as of 2026-10-05 (devguide); end of life 2029-10.

Free-threaded build officially supported (PEP 779), template strings (PEP 750), deferred annotations (PEP 649/749), subinterpreters in the stdlib (PEP 734). Current bugfix line: 3.14.8 on 2026-09-30; end of life 2030-10.
Third release candidate, added to the schedule after rc2 (PEP 790 lists it under 'Actual').

Expected final (PEP 790). Headline PEPs in What's New: explicit lazy imports (810), frozendict (814), sentinel (661), a profiling package with the Tachyon sampling profiler (799), frame pointers on by default (831), stable ABI for free-threaded builds (803), UTF-8 default encoding (686). End of life about 2031-10.
First release date listed for 3.16 on the devguide (PEP 826).
ISO/IEC 14882:2017 (cppreference lists the year; the month is not shown there, so only the year is claimed). Structured bindings, std::optional, std::variant, if constexpr.
Concepts, ranges, coroutines, modules, three-way comparison, std::span, std::format.
GCC 11.1: 'The default mode for C++ is now -std=gnu++17 instead of -std=gnu++14.'

Clang 16 release notes: 'Clang's default C++/ObjC++ standard is now gnu++17 instead of gnu++14.' Apple's Xcode clang is a separate fork: measured here, Apple clang 14.0.0 reports __cplusplus 199711L and the Command Line Tools' Apple clang 17.0.0 reports 201402L when no -std flag is given.

Published by ISO as ISO/IEC 14882:2024 in October 2024 (ISO page, archived capture). std::expected, std::print, std::mdspan, deducing this, import std. MSVC still exposes it as /std:c++23preview (MSVC Build Tools preview notes, September 2026).

Herb Sutter, 2026-03-29: 'C++26 is done!' at the London Croydon meeting: static reflection, contracts, std::execution, the hardened standard library and no undefined behaviour for reading uninitialised locals. Then the DIS ballot; cppreference lists final draft N5050 dated 2026-06-01. ISO publication was not confirmed on 2026-10-05.
GCC 16.1: 'GCC 16 changes the default language version for C++ compilation from -std=gnu++17 to -std=gnu++20.' C++20 modules still need -fmodules. Latest: GCC 16.2 on 2026-08-07.
Brno: adopted a catalogue of all undefined behaviour in C++ (P3596) as a step toward addressing it in C++29, plus work on safety profiles.
Shipped with Rust 1.31.0 (RFC 2052, which also created editions): the module-system changes, async becomes a keyword.
Shipped with Rust 1.56.0 (RFC 3085): disjoint closure captures, IntoIterator for arrays, resolver 2 by default.
Shipped with Rust 1.85.0 (RFC 3501). cargo new on Rust 1.99 writes edition = "2024" (measured). No later edition had been announced on the Rust blog index on 2026-10-05.

Current stable. A new stable every six weeks: 1.97.0 on 2026-07-09, 1.98.0 on 2026-08-20, 1.99.0 on 2026-10-01 (RELEASES.md). Editions are chosen per crate and crates of different editions link together.
Classes, modules, let/const, arrow functions, promises: the big one. Every edition since is yearly, each June.
async functions, shared memory and atomics, Object.values/entries.
Optional chaining (?.), nullish coalescing (??), BigInt, dynamic import(), globalThis.
Top-level await, class fields and private #fields, .at(), Error cause.
Object.groupBy / Map.groupBy, Promise.withResolvers, resizable ArrayBuffers, RegExp v flag.
Iterator helpers, new Set methods, JSON modules and import attributes, Promise.try, RegExp.escape, Float16.
Array.fromAsync, Error.isError, Math.sumPrecise, Uint8Array to and from Base64, upsert (Map getOrInsert), iterator sequencing, JSON.parse source text access.
Already at Stage 4 for 2027: Temporal, explicit resource management (using), joint iteration, iterator chunking and join. Node 26 already enables Temporal by default.
Standard decorators, const type parameters. First stable 5.0.x on npm.
Node 22 (Jod) enters LTS; it later gains type stripping on by default in 22.18.0. Maintenance since 2025-10-21, end of life 2027-04-30.
Last 5.x minor (5.9.2 on npm).
Node 24 (Krypton) Active LTS; type stripping marked stable in 24.12.0. Maintenance from 2026-10-20, end of life 2028-04-30.
The last compiler written in TypeScript: new defaults (strict on, module esnext, types []) and deprecations, to prepare for 7.0. 6.0.3 on 2026-04-16 is the latest 6.x.
Current line, V8 14.6, Temporal on by default. Planned LTS 2026-10-28. From Node 27 the cycle is annual and every major becomes LTS.

The Go port (formerly tsgo, Project Corsa) becomes the typescript package and its tsc: Microsoft reports 8x to 12x faster full builds (VS Code 125.7 s to 10.6 s). No programmatic API until 7.1, so tools like typescript-eslint, Vue, Svelte and Astro tooling keep TypeScript 6 alongside (@typescript/typescript6, binary tsc6). Latest 7.0.2.
Scheduled start of LTS for Node 26.

notes.method: Each version is the newest stable release on the official registry or release page, read on 2026-10-05 by research/fetch_versions.py (PyPI JSON API, crates.io API, npm registry, GitHub release feeds) or from the page linked.
